This is the first post on the research blog, and mostly a test of the toolchain: math via
MathJax, citations via BibTeX, and an executable code cell producing a figure — the things
this blog needs for writing up graph ML experiments.

## Math

A simple way to think about graph embedding is as a map $f: V \to \mathbb{R}^d$ from nodes
to vectors that preserves structural similarity. One common training objective,
following the skip-gram formulation used in @grover2016node2vec, is

$$
\mathcal{L} = -\sum_{u \in V} \sum_{v \in N(u)} \log \frac{\exp(f(u)^\top f(v))}{\sum_{w \in V} \exp(f(u)^\top f(w))}.
$$

Graph convolutional approaches such as @kipf2017semi instead learn embeddings by
propagating and transforming neighbor features layer by layer:

$$
H^{(l+1)} = \sigma\left(\tilde{D}^{-\frac{1}{2}} \tilde{A} \tilde{D}^{-\frac{1}{2}} H^{(l)} W^{(l)}\right).
$$

## An executable figure

A toy graph, laid out in 2D as a stand-in for a learned embedding:

```{python}
#| label: fig-toy-embedding
#| fig-cap: "Spring layout of a small random graph, used here as a toy 2D embedding."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import networkx as nx

G = nx.karate_club_graph()
pos = nx.spring_layout(G, seed=7)
colors = ["#4C72B0" if G.nodes[n]["club"] == "Mr. Hi" else "#DD8452" for n in G.nodes]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 5))
nx.draw_networkx(G, pos, node_color=colors, edge_color="#cccccc", with_labels=False, node_size=120, ax=ax)
ax.set_axis_off()
plt.show()
```

Nodes cluster by club membership even without any learning — a reminder that a good
layout algorithm and a good embedding model are solving related problems.
